title: Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing

concept.text: The innovation would be a practical programmable computer that preserves information through reversible operations and recovers much of the energy used to switch its logic and memory. A reversible operation retains enough information to reconstruct its input from its output. Making that property useful requires physical circuits that return switching energy for reuse, together with an architecture that maintains the savings while running complete programs.

Logical reversibility and low physical dissipation are related but distinct. Preserving information does not automatically recover energy, eliminate losses, or make a computer consume zero power. Landauer’s limit concerns the minimum work associated with logically irreversible information erasure under the relevant thermodynamic conditions. A practical system must still account for finite-time circuit losses, control, memory, communication, and whatever information it ultimately erases. Hybrid architectures combining reversible operations with necessary irreversible operations are therefore relevant to this concept.

Proposed system scope: the breakthrough encompasses fast, reliable, densely integrated logic and memory, energy-recovering clocks and control, interconnects, input/output, and the management of temporary information. Its defining outcome would be a substantial measured reduction in total energy per correctly completed task at useful performance. An efficient isolated gate would be a component of that achievement, rather than sufficient evidence of the complete innovation.

significance.text: If a programmable architecture could retain large energy savings across complete workloads, it could perform more computation within a fixed power and cooling budget. That would change an important constraint on computing capacity: the energy required to produce useful results. Tang and colleagues’ work motivates this direction through efficient gate operations, but the architecture-wide benefit remains conditional on successful integration and measurement.

Conditional downstream possibilities include greater computing capacity at power-constrained facilities, lower operating energy for a given workload, or longer operation from a limited energy supply. These are synthesis-level consequences of a sufficiently large total-energy advantage, not forecasts established by the supplied papers. Their magnitude would depend on throughput, hardware cost, workload suitability, and whether memory, communication, control, or cooling become the dominant expenses.

The thermodynamic distinction matters to the scale of the claim. Reversible computing would not abolish the energy cost of computation or make necessary erasure free. Nor does recovering switching energy establish that a system will outperform competitive conventional hardware. The revolutionary outcome would be a useful computing architecture whose savings survive all relevant overheads, including any cooling required by its physical implementation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability in the supplied evidence is an integrated programmable system that combines energy recovery with useful speed, accuracy, and total-energy savings. Tang and colleagues analyze the tradeoffs among work, speed, and fidelity in simulated gate protocols. Their finite-time operations incur dissipation, and their discussion identifies more complex reversible primitives as future work. The study therefore supports a technical path toward the innovation without establishing that the system-level objective has been achieved.

Proposed engineering requirements: recover switching energy without making operations impractically slow; maintain sufficiently low error rates in the presence of noise and device variation; and integrate enough logic and memory to execute substantial programs. Recovered energy must remain useful after clock distribution, control, interconnect, and input/output losses. For superconducting implementations, the accounting must also include the energy required to maintain operating conditions. These are system-design barriers inferred from the objective, rather than a complete checklist established by the supplied article.

Proposed architectural requirements: programs must manage intermediate information, memory reuse, initialization, and eventual erasure without consuming the gains obtained in individual operations. Reliability mechanisms and error recovery must also fit within the energy budget. The unresolved challenge is to make these functions work together at useful scale; demonstrating information preservation in one operation does not establish efficient execution of a complete computation.

current_state.text: The supplied research dates Kuen Wai Tang, Kyle J. Ray, and James P. Crutchfield’s “Momentum-driven reversible logic accelerates efficient irreversible universal computation” to 2 September 2026. The validated review identifies its results as simulations of operations in coupled superconducting quantum flux parametrons. The study analyzes two-bit gate protocols, including controlled erasure and a physically embedded NAND operation, and estimates work and fidelity from simulated trajectories and ensembles. These are gate-level computational results, not measurements from a constructed programmable processor.

Tang and colleagues compare hybrid reversible/irreversible gate operations and describe their protocol as ready for experimental realization. That characterization expresses a proposed next step, rather than an experimental demonstration. Their analysis relates minimum work to entropy change and reports finite-time protocols that cost more than the relevant minimum. It does not demonstrate wall-plug savings, integrated memory and control, or a whole-system advantage over conventional computers. The validated review had the full main article text, but supplementary material and figure graphics were not supplied for inspection.

The earlier research record attributes a 1 June 2026 paper, “Quantum Landauer erasure using magnetic tunneling junctions,” to Chuncheng Wang and colleagues. It describes a magnetic-memory reset experiment combining measurements and simulation, with estimated quasi-adiabatic reset dissipation near the Landauer scale, and says an indexed abstract and metadata were available while direct publisher-PDF access failed. However, the saved PubMed material available to the validated review contained only a cookie challenge. Consequently, that review could not verify the publication’s identity, experimental details, or energy estimate. The reported result remains unresolved in this evidence set; the access failure is not evidence that it is false.

Even if the attributed Wang result is confirmed, a memory-reset experiment would address the energetics of erasure rather than demonstrate a reversible processor. Likewise, the verified Tang simulations do not establish the proposed integrated computing system. The supplied bounded search record is empty, so these materials do not establish comprehensive coverage of the field or whether the full objective remained open as of 1 November 2026. This coverage limitation does not invalidate the dated Tang results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: construct a programmable system and run a predefined suite of representative workloads at explicitly specified useful throughput and reliability. Compare wall-plug energy per correctly completed task against competitive conventional systems under matched task, output-quality, and performance requirements. Define the required substantial energy advantage before testing. The supplied evidence does not establish a numerical threshold or a consensus standard for declaring this innovation complete.
completion_criteria.label: Programmable workloads demonstrate predefined substantial wall-plug energy advantage

completion_criteria.text: Proposed accounting boundary: include logic, memory, control, clock generation and distribution, data movement, input/output, cooling, initialization, and necessary information erasure. Measure long enough to capture recurring preparation and reset costs, and disclose which equipment and energy flows fall inside the boundary. Component measurements should show that energy recovery contributes to the observed advantage, while the decisive comparison remains total energy for the completed task.
completion_criteria.label: Full task energy accounting demonstrates contributions from energy recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independent investigators should be able to reproduce the energy, throughput, and correctness results using documented hardware, control procedures, workloads, baselines, and measurement uncertainties. Tests should examine relevant operating conditions, sustained operation, and changes in workload or system scale. Report where the advantage narrows or disappears. A finite workload suite would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality or an advantage for every computation.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction confirms system results and reports energy advantage limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ELE-08, “Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics,” overlaps most directly through the goal of reducing switching energy. Its defining capability is manufacturable low-voltage operation; ELE-04 centers on preserving information and recovering energy. The approaches could be complementary, but either would need its own demonstration. ELE-11, “Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage,” shares the requirement that component improvements survive system overheads, while pursuing a different physical computing platform. Neither entry should be merged with reversible computing.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-01, “Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors,” overlaps through superconducting physics and possible reductions in resistive losses. Tang’s superconducting circuit proposal does not establish ambient-temperature superconductivity, and reversible computing need not depend on that breakthrough. ELE-02, “Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation,” also concerns information processing and reliability, but reversible logic alone does not establish quantum computation or fault tolerance. ELE-03, “A long-distance quantum repeater network,” concerns quantum communication across distance rather than energy recovery in a processor.

Roster-based synthesis: ELE-05, “Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply,” ELE-07, “Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery,” and ELE-09, “Resilient, self-restoring power networks,” address energy storage, delivery, and infrastructure resilience. Reversible computing could conditionally reduce demand on such systems, but it would not supply their missing capabilities. ELE-10, “Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing,” could benefit from lower computation energy, although sensing, communication, and energy collection would remain separate constraints. ELE-06, “Durable, high-bandwidth two-way neural interface,” could likewise benefit from efficient supporting electronics, while its defining interface capabilities remain distinct.

unresolved_issues: The Wang publication’s identity, methods, dissipation estimate, and uncertainty remain unverified in the material available to the validated review. The discrepancy between reported abstract access and the saved cookie challenge is unresolved.
Tang’s supplementary material and figure graphics were not supplied for inspection, limiting assessment beyond the retained main article text.
The empty bounded search record leaves field-wide completeness and continued openness as of 1 November 2026 unassessed.
A completion program still needs explicit workload selection, throughput and reliability requirements, comparison baselines, measurement boundaries, and a predefined minimum energy advantage.

brief.title: Computers that reuse energy as they calculate
possible: People could run programs using substantially less electricity, or do more computing with the same power supply. The computer would reuse much of the energy spent changing its internal states. Its reversible operations would preserve enough information to reconstruct their inputs from their outputs.
why: Computing facilities could fit more work within their power and cooling budgets. Devices with limited energy supplies could run longer. The benefit would come from reducing the energy needed for a useful result across a complete program.

sources.showed: They report magnetic memory resets close to the Landauer limit, the theoretical minimum heat released when erasing information. Their work combines measurements with simulations.
sources.quote: In this work, we construct a quantum thermodynamic framework for erasure in MTJs and experimentally confirm the Landauer limit in nanoscale memory cells.
sources.cited_for: The study supports approaching the minimum heat cost of erasure in magnetic memory.
sources.not_established: An efficient memory reset does not demonstrate energy recovery or savings across a programmable computer.

sources.who: Kuen Wai Tang, Kyle J. Ray and James P. Crutchfield
sources.showed: Their simulations compared basic logic operations. A design using momentum, the system's continuing motion, ran faster and produced correct outputs more often without extra energy cost.
sources.quote:
simultaneously achieving higher ﬁdelity and faster computational speed
without incurring any additional energetic cost.
sources.cited_for: The simulations support combining information-preserving operations with necessary erasure to improve basic computation.
sources.not_established: The work does not demonstrate a physical programmable processor or total electricity savings.

shown: Tang and colleagues have simulated promising basic operations, but have not built a programmable processor demonstrating the proposed savings. Wang and colleagues report a physical memory-reset experiment; that addresses erasure rather than a complete reversible computer.
missing: A programmable computer must recover energy while running substantial programs at useful speed and accuracy.
Savings must survive memory, control, data movement, cooling and other costs across the whole machine.
Programs must manage temporary information, memory reuse and eventual erasure without spending the recovered energy.

milestones.label: Complete programs use substantially less electricity
milestones.explanation: A programmable system would have to beat competitive conventional computers on total electricity per correct task at matched performance, using a predefined savings target. This would establish a useful advantage.

milestones.label: Full energy accounting confirms recovery contributes to savings
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to include every task-related energy cost and show that recovered energy contributes to the savings. This would connect efficient operations to the whole machine's advantage.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and identify their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce energy use, speed and correctness, and report where the advantage shrinks or disappears. This would establish how reliably and broadly the savings hold.

uncertain: Preserving information does not automatically recover energy; how much recovery can survive useful-speed operation remains open.
The workloads, performance requirements and minimum savings needed to declare success still need explicit definitions.
The advantage may depend on the workload, operating conditions and machine size.

page.title: Energy-recovering reversible computing
page.definition: A programmable computer uses logically reversible operations, whose inputs can be reconstructed from their outputs, and recovers switching energy for reuse. It completes a specified workload with less total supplied energy than a conventional computer meeting the same output and performance requirements.

goal.need: Data centres consumed an estimated 415 TWh of electricity in 2024. The goal is to reduce energy per completed computation by reusing switching energy. IEEE identifies design overheads and parasitic losses as obstacles to preserving component savings across a complete system.

statements.body: IEEE International Roadmap for Devices and Systems
statements.quote: Realizing the energy efficiency promise of reversible computing at a system level remains a significant engineering hurdle.

statements.body: JSPS KAKENHI project 19H05614, Yokohama National University
statements.quote: The goal of the project is to realize a low-power reversible AQFP processor.
statements.context: AQFP means adiabatic quantum flux parametron, a superconducting logic device driven by gradually varying magnetic flux.

completion.title: A programmable reversible computer uses less total energy for a workload at matched performance.
completion.criterion: A fabricated programmable computer completes a specified workload with less total supplied energy than a conventional computer meeting the same output, latency and throughput requirements. The energy boundary includes logic, memory, clock generation and distribution, control, communication, input/output, initialization, erasure and cooling. The reduction exceeds measurement uncertainty, and circuit measurements establish switching-energy recovery. The benchmark and conventional comparator are specified before measurement. This is an Atlas test; no minimum percentage saving or absolute operating speed is prescribed.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; synthesis of the system-level objectives in IEEE IRDS and Sandia’s research challenges.
completion.basis: IEEE IRDS, DOE EES2, Sandia, JSPS and developer material were searched for a complete-program energy and performance acceptance test. None was found. SCSP proposes a 20-fold processor performance-per-power improvement, but gives no workload or total-energy boundary. The narrower Atlas test requires a measured net saving across the complete system.

milestones.title: Fabricated reversible logic gates recover their input states through inverse operations.
milestones.criterion: A fabricated gate implements a one-to-one mapping and its inverse restores the input; reverse data propagation tests physical bidirectionality. Takeuchi and colleagues demonstrated three-input superconducting RQFP gates in three experimental configurations at 100 kHz and 4.2 K, published on 15 September 2014. Their gate-energy results were simulations. Wang and colleagues’ magnetic-tunnel-junction reset experiment concerns information erasure and does not establish this gate test.
milestones.set_by: Takeuchi, Yamanashi and Yoshikawa, experiments β and γ in Scientific Reports. The published protocol concerns superconducting RQFP gates; input restoration is the corresponding test for either platform.
milestones.threshold_quote: two RQFP gates are connected but one is physically mirrored to demonstrate physical reversibility.

milestones.title: An energy-recovering circuit operates with an energy-recovery factor greater than 1.
milestones.criterion: Using Vaire’s definition, the recovery factor Rf equals logic signal energy divided by energy dissipated per cycle. Positive recovery efficiency, η = 1 − 1/Rf, requires Rf > 1. Vaire reported factors of 1.77 for a capacitor array and 1.41 for a shift register on its 22 nm CMOS Ice River chip at a 500 MHz data frequency. These company results were reported in an interview published on 3 September 2025 and are not peer reviewed. They establish component recovery, not total computer energy savings.
milestones.set_by: Vaire, The Technology of Near-Zero Energy Computing, page 10, defines recovery efficiency. Its CTO’s interview records Rf > 1 as the proof-of-concept threshold for CMOS.
milestones.threshold_quote: For a traditional system with an R-factor of 1, efficiency is 0: no energy is recovered.

milestones.title: A programmable processor completes a program with integrated reversible logic and energy recovery.
milestones.criterion: A fabricated processor integrates reversible logic, memory, control and an energy-recovering supply and completes a program with its specified output. No minimum clock rate, memory capacity or numerical error rate is imposed. No qualifying integrated result was located for either platform. Tang and colleagues report two-bit superconducting gate simulations, including an Erasure-Flip comparison with 10^7 simulated particles; these do not establish processor integration.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; no cross-platform integration acceptance protocol was found in IEEE IRDS, Sandia’s research challenges or JSPS project 19H05614.

not_found: No published acceptance test was found specifying complete workloads, matched performance and total supplied energy for a reversible computer.
The 2014 IEEE second Rebooting Computing Summit report could not be opened, so its indexed demonstration targets are not used as thresholds.
A primary semiconductor experiment applying the same inverse-operation and bidirectionality protocol as the RQFP demonstration was not located.
A superconducting demonstration meeting the stated net circuit energy-recovery test was not located.
A peer-reviewed measurement report, device sample size and uncertainty budget for Ice River’s recovery factors were not located.
The full publisher text of Wang and colleagues’ magnetic-tunnel-junction erasure paper could not be opened.

results.finding: A simulated two-bit Erasure-Flip gate produced 2 errors across 10 million trajectories.
results.detail: The gate combines reversible and irreversible operations. It was simulated, and the paper does not report a fabricated processor integrating memory, control and an energy-recovering supply.
results.quote:
Across 107 trajectories, only two errors were observed, and
these originated from the erasure pair rather than the storage pair.

results.finding: Fabricated three-input superconducting RQFP gates recovered inputs in inverse and reverse-propagation tests across 3 experimental configurations.
results.detail: Experiments ran at 100 kHz and 4.2 K. Two serially connected gates tested logical reversibility; mirroring one tested bidirectional propagation. Gate-energy dissipation was simulated, not measured.
results.quote: Similarly, the outputs corresponded to the inputs in γ, which proves its physical reversibility. These results confirm that the RQFP gate is logically and physically reversible, and that the RQFP gate is a practical reversible logic gate.

results.finding: One fabricated 350 nm CMOS chip containing reversible adder cascades produced no errors for the tested input vectors.
results.detail: The chip cascaded adders with mirrored subtractors to compute and uncompute an identity function. The text does not establish a test in which data propagated backward through the same physical gate to restore its input.
results.quote:
When properly measured alone, the cascaded identity
blocks chip gives very good results, introducing no error
whatever are the chosen input vectors.

results.finding: One CMOS test chip’s nRERL serial multiplier consumed 0.9% of the energy of a static CMOS comparator.
results.detail: At 100 kHz and 5 V, the measured consumption included the clocked power generator. The source does not report logic signal energy or a recovery factor, so Rf > 1 cannot be established.
results.quote:
plier consumed only /0/./9 /#25 of the energy consumed in the
static CMOS one at /1/0/0 kHz/, where the adiabatic and
leak age losses w ere ab out equal/.

results.finding: One 8-bit CMOS nRERL microprocessor integrated an eight-phase clocked power generator; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The fabricated chip included logic, memory, control and a clocked power generator, and energy was measured during a test program. The text does not report program completion with a specified output. Some logic reversibility was deliberately broken.
results.quote:
We integrated an 8-bit nRERL microprocessor with an 8-phase 
clocked power generator into a chip with 0.25 µm CMOS 
technology.
